package_info.package_versions: N/A (APT campaign, not a public package)
package_info.why_malicious: ThreatNeedle is a custom malware family attributed to the North Korean APT group Lazarus, specifically designed for targeted espionage against defense industry organizations. It leverages spear-phishing emails with Covid-19 themes and personalized lures to gain initial access, then deploys a multi-stage payload that establishes persistence, enables lateral movement, and exfiltrates sensitive data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

execution_context.file_location: dropped executable on victim machine (e.g., %APPDATA%\[random].exe or C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Roaming\[random].exe)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Custom ThreatNeedle malware binary that, once executed, establishes a command-and-control (C2) channel to attacker infrastructure, enumerates files and directories on the system, collects sensitive documents, and exfiltrates them over the network. The malware also implements persistence mechanisms and may inject into legitimate processes to evade detection.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-compromise, after payload execution), the code establishes a persistent outbound C2 connection to a remote attacker-controlled server, enumerates files and directories on the victim system, collects and exfiltrates selected data, and may inject into legitimate processes to evade detection, resulting in unauthorized data theft and ongoing remote access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Establishing a persistent C2 channel, enumerating and exfiltrating files, and injecting into legitimate processes are hallmark behaviors of advanced espionage malware. The use of custom binaries and persistence mechanisms further indicates targeted malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not open persistent outbound connections to unknown servers, enumerate and exfiltrate user files without consent, or inject code into other processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools may establish outbound connections and enumerate files, but only with explicit user consent, to trusted endpoints, and without process injection or data exfiltration to untrusted infrastructure.
key_indicators: Outbound C2 traffic to known or suspicious Lazarus/ThreatNeedle infrastructure
Automated enumeration and exfiltration of files and directories
Execution of dropped binaries from spear-phishing email context
Persistence via registry modifications or scheduled tasks
Process injection into legitimate system processes

execution_context.file_location: malicious document or executable attached to spear-phishing email (e.g., Covid-19 themed .doc or .xls file)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Covid-19 themed spear-phishing document containing an embedded VBA macro or exploit shellcode that, when triggered by the user, writes the ThreatNeedle malware binary to disk and executes it, initiating the infection chain.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon user opening the malicious attachment (initial infection), the embedded macro or exploit executes, writes the ThreatNeedle malware binary to disk, and launches it as a new process, resulting in the installation and execution of the main malware payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Malicious macros or exploits embedded in documents are a common initial access vector for APT campaigns. The use of Covid-19 themed lures and automated payload delivery is indicative of targeted spear-phishing.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate documents should not contain macros or exploits that drop and execute binaries, especially without user awareness or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Macros may be used for business process automation, but not for writing and executing arbitrary binaries from document context.
key_indicators: Covid-19 themed document attachments with embedded macros or exploits
Execution of macros or shellcode upon document opening
Dropping and execution of unknown binaries from document process
Initiation of new processes from Office or document viewer context

attack_chain.action: Victim receives a spear-phishing email with a Covid-19 themed attachment containing a malicious macro or exploit.
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens the attachment, triggering the embedded macro or exploit.

attack_chain.action: The malicious macro or exploit executes, writing the ThreatNeedle malware binary to disk and launching it as a new process.
attack_chain.leads_to: ThreatNeedle malware is installed and executed on the victim machine.

attack_chain.action: ThreatNeedle malware establishes a persistent C2 connection, enumerates files and directories, collects sensitive data, and exfiltrates it to attacker infrastructure. The malware may also establish persistence and inject into legitimate processes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Espionage, data theft, and ongoing remote access by the attacker.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of macros or exploits from Covid-19 themed document attachments
Dropping and execution of unknown binaries from Office or document viewer processes
Creation of persistence mechanisms (e.g., registry run keys, scheduled tasks) by unknown binaries
Outbound C2 connections to suspicious or known Lazarus/ThreatNeedle infrastructure
Automated enumeration and exfiltration of files and directories
Process injection by unknown binaries into legitimate system processes
file_indicators: Covid-19 themed document attachments with embedded macros or exploit code
Dropped executables with uncommon, random, or obfuscated filenames in user profile or AppData directories
Persistence artifacts such as registry run keys or scheduled tasks referencing unknown executables
Malicious documents with macro code that writes and executes binaries
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known Lazarus/ThreatNeedle C2 domains or IP addresses as listed in threat intelligence feeds
Unusual traffic patterns to remote servers immediately after document opening
Encrypted or obfuscated network traffic from unknown executables
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of macros or exploits in document attachments, especially those with Covid-19 themes. Detect dropped and executed binaries originating from Office or document viewer processes. Analyze endpoint persistence mechanisms for references to unknown executables. Monitor outbound network traffic for connections to known Lazarus/ThreatNeedle C2 infrastructure or anomalous destinations. Use endpoint detection to flag automated file enumeration, exfiltration behaviors, and process injection by unknown binaries.
